message: Batch FAISS uint8 candidate reconstruction before rescoring
head: ceba445678cdbda149cac7e8090d329f017e2d34
title: Batch FAISS uint8 candidate reconstruction before rescoring
body:
## Change

Batch reconstruction of uint8 FAISS candidates before rescoring, using the floating-point index's native `reconstruct_batch` API. The current nested Python loop makes one call per retrieved vector. Binary indexes keep their existing per-vector path because they do not expose this API.

This was found through code analysis and measured with real FAISS indexes. The change preserves candidate selection, calibration, returned keys/scores, and filtering of padded `-1` results. It builds on the scalar rescoring calibration in #4058 and the padding handling in #3887; it does not propose a new quantization scheme.

## Validation

[Independent CPU validation and benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43903476519/job/133425986469) checks unchanged base `9ac7fdb4` and exact candidate `ceba4456`.

- 13 new compatibility cases pass on both revisions: Flat, HNSW and IDMap indexes, noncontiguous document keys, single/multiple queries, short result sets and an empty index.
- `pytest tests/util/test_quantization.py tests/util/test_faiss_batch_reconstruction.py -q`: **171 passed**, including real FAISS and USearch tests.
- `pytest tests/util/test_retrieval.py -k semantic_search -q`: **49 passed**, 153 unrelated cases deselected.
- `pre-commit run --all-files` and `git diff --check`: passed.

The [reproducible benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/blob/f087887f0be0530c2b94c50a8e3e314846a3a2d8/.validation/st-faiss-benchmark.py) measures complete calls against a reused FlatIP index: 128 queries, 128 dimensions, top 50, 2× rescoring, one CPU thread, three warmups and nine timed runs.

| Corpus vectors | Before median | After median | Ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5,000 | 46.75 ms | 22.93 ms | 2.04× |
| 50,000 | 136.34 ms | 112.73 ms | 1.21× |

Every returned document ID and score has an identical digest before/after. This is a synthetic embedding retrieval benchmark, not encoder throughput; no memory or GPU improvement is claimed. Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.6.0 CPU, NumPy 2.3.5, FAISS 1.16.0. The full model/training suite and older FAISS versions were not run.

message: Stabilize LambdaLoss gains for finite relevance scores
head: 7bc2a876eb80b7a246fafbe7f9425691d97314cd
title: Stabilize LambdaLoss gains across finite relevance ranges
body:
## Problem

`LambdaLoss` forms NDCG gains as `2**relevance - 1` in float32. Finite relevance scores can therefore produce either overflowing gains or cancellation to zero. This affects listwise training with continuous teacher scores, including unnormalized dot-product scores or scores scaled close to zero.

Found through code analysis and reproduced with the public loss API. With predicted scores `[0, 1, 2]`:

- relevance `[130, 129, 0]`: loss and gradients are NaN on main; the corrected loss is approximately **3.298718** with finite gradients;
- relevance `[1e-8, 0, 0]`: main returns zero loss and gradients despite the ordering; the corrected loss is approximately **6.396224**.

The reproduction and tests use a trainable lookup scorer, not a claim of a production training incident.

## Change

Factor a common power of two out of the gains and ideal DCG, and evaluate the small difference with `expm1`. The factor cancels in the normalized gain. The epsilon floor is scaled by the same factor, preserving its original meaning. Weighting schemes, pair selection and loss reduction remain unchanged.

This is separate from #4116, which stabilized the log-sigmoid of predicted score differences; the failure here is in relevance gains before weighting.

## Validation

[Independent validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43903476519/job/133425987120) checks exact base `9ac7fdb4` and candidate `7bc2a876`.

- New regressions on unchanged base: **98 failed, 144 passed**.
- The same regressions after the fix: **242 passed**.
- `pytest tests/cross_encoder/losses/test_misc.py tests/cross_encoder/losses/test_lambda_gain_precision.py -q`: **354 passed, 6 skipped**. The skips are the existing CUDA-only float16 CrossEncoder cases; CPU bfloat16 checks run.
- `pre-commit run --all-files` and `git diff --check`: passed.

The independent oracle computes gains with 80-digit Decimal arithmetic and enumerates pair weights. It compares both losses and parameter gradients across all five weighting schemes, top-k choices, both logarithm bases, large/small/ordinary relevance values, ties, zero/negative labels, padding, and a non-default epsilon.

Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.6.0 CPU, Transformers 5.23.0. The full repository suite, GPU execution and minimum dependency matrix were not run.

head: a08bf4d023f8b9b2de154a45c8dd36234044fd78
title: Support mixed tensor and NumPy dtypes in multi-vector scoring
body:
## Problem

A bfloat16 MultiVectorEncoder returns bfloat16 tensors when `convert_to_numpy=False`, but its NumPy export uses float32. Scoring those queries against exported documents currently raises a matrix-multiplication dtype error. The same mismatch affects MaxSim, MeanMaxSim and XTR, including their pairwise APIs.

This was identified by code analysis and reproduced through `WordEmbeddings` + `MultiVectorEncoder.encode_query/encode_document`, with no model download. The regression includes that public workflow, rather than only calling internal scoring helpers.

## Change

Promote query and document embeddings to their common PyTorch dtype immediately before token matrix multiplication. Uniform dtypes retain their existing path and output dtype. Masks, normalization, chunk boundaries and gradient propagation are preserved. Applying the conversion before the MaxSim callback also covers the optional kernel route.

The optional kernel API was introduced in #4344. This change handles mixed query/document dtypes produced by the encoder's own tensor/NumPy export options.

## Validation

[Independent CPU validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43908295487) uses unchanged base `9ac7fdb4` and exact candidate `a08bf4d0`, with PyTorch 2.6.0 and Python 3.12:

- On the unchanged baseline, the 40 new cases produce **36 failures and 4 passes** in both environments.
- On the candidate, the new cases plus similarity and multi-vector loss tests produce **245 passes and 6 existing skips** in each environment.
- The selected XTR/MaxSim/ColBERT model tests produce **30 passes**, 126 unrelated cases deselected, in each environment.
- With Transformers 5.20.0 and kernels 0.17.2, the optional kernel suite produces **106 passes and 56 existing skips**. The second environment uses Transformers 5.23.0 without the optional kernel package.
- All repository pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass in both environments.

Coverage includes float16/bfloat16/float32/float64 pairs, masks, rectangular and pairwise scores, chunking, all three XTR scorers, independently computed MaxSim scores and gradients, and unchanged uniform-bfloat16 behavior. GPU execution and the full repository suite were not run.

AI assistance: OpenAI Codex helped with investigation, implementation, regression tests and this description.

head: c8af6717da005b8b2b578a0ef72b65bc000db349
title: Reduce SPLADE max-pooling inference work before logarithms
body:
## Change

For SPLADE max pooling with gradients disabled, reduce masked token logits over the sequence dimension before applying ReLU and log1p. These monotone transforms produce the same maximum, while only the pooled vocabulary vector needs the logarithms. Both padded/chunked and flattened inputs use this path.

Training keeps the existing transform-before-pool order: finite-precision log1p can turn distinct logits into ties, so reordering that path could change which token receives a gradient. Sum pooling is unchanged.

This was found through code analysis and measured using the public SpladePooling module. SparseEncoder.encode already executes its forward pass under inference mode, so normal encoding uses the optimization.

## Validation

[Independent exact-base validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43910447407) compares base `9ac7fdb4` with candidate `c8af6717`:

- **101 passed** on both baseline and candidate, independently with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**.
- **264 passed** selected public SparseEncoder tests in each environment, covering query/document encoding, decoding, sparsity and the chunk-size setting; 98 unrelated cases deselected.
- All repository pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass in both environments.

Compatibility cases cover both activation functions; float16, bfloat16, float32 and float64; uneven chunks; left/right padding; entirely masked rows; flattened sequences; caller-input preservation; CPU autocast; and training gradients at rounding-induced ties.

The [reproducible benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/blob/c08595ecb28cc873c52206148abde9d56d0dccf9/.validation/st-splade-max-benchmark.py) measures complete pooling calls on synthetic MLM logits: two documents, 256 padded tokens, vocabulary size 30,522, float32, one CPU thread, three warmups and nine timed runs. Flattened inputs contain 224 and 256 tokens.

| PyTorch 2.14.1 case | Before median | After median | Ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Padded, ReLU + log1p | 56.46 ms | 41.66 ms | 1.36× |
| Padded, double log1p, chunk 64 | 60.48 ms | 35.19 ms | 1.72× |
| Flattened, ReLU + log1p | 18.87 ms | 6.62 ms | 2.85× |
| Flattened, double log1p | 31.64 ms | 7.00 ms | 4.52× |

All output digests are identical before/after. The same four cases on PyTorch 2.6.0 measured 1.44×, 1.89×, 4.87× and 7.92×. These are component timings with precomputed logits, not encoder throughput; GPU performance and peak memory were not measured.

head: bb300ecbd87fa6a8a449118fb45cadac2ce4a6eb
title: Avoid broadcasted GIST cosine matrices during training
body:
## Change

Compute the default GIST cosine-similarity matrix by normalizing each embedding once and multiplying the two matrices. GISTEmbedLoss and CachedGISTEmbedLoss currently broadcast to a batch-by-batch-by-dimension tensor, including tensors retained for backward. The shared helper removes that expansion.

The optimized path handles matching float32/float64 inputs on CPU/CUDA. Other dtypes, custom similarity modules and non-default dimensions retain their existing path. Autocast is disabled for the matrix product to preserve float32 inputs. The norm clamp remains outside autograd, matching CosineSimilarity's derivative for norms below eps.

This was identified through code analysis and reproduced through the public loss classes with precomputed embeddings. It is separate from the positive/self-pair masking fix in #4284 and distributed gathering in #4223.

## Validation

[Exact-base comparison on PyTorch 2.6.0 and 2.14.1](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43912070038) checks base `9ac7fdb4` and candidate `bb300ecb`:

- **88 passed** on both baseline and candidate in each environment, including existing GIST/CachedGIST tests, full loss values and embedding gradients, rectangular/non-contiguous inputs, both margin strategies, tiny norms, configured eps, mixed/low-precision fallbacks, custom similarity classes and CPU autocast.
- Independent native float64 cosine references cover input scales 1e-10, 1 and 1e8. For the tiny-scale float32 diagnostic, gradient norm-relative errors against float64 were 2.7e-8 to 9.2e-8 for the candidate across both PyTorch versions; native float32 errors were 5.4e-8 to 9.7e-8. The test checks normwise accuracy rather than relative error of an individual cancellation-prone coordinate.
- Every repository pre-commit hook and `git diff --check` passes in both environments.

The [reproducible benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/blob/3cde827942f143df82caada3c1a966cca19d2fbc/.validation/st-gist-cosine-benchmark.py) measures complete loss forward/backward operations with fixed precomputed embeddings, one CPU thread, two warmups and seven timed runs. Losses and gradients are checked against the baseline.

| PyTorch 2.14.1 case | Before median | After median | Ratio | Saved tensor storage before / after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| GIST, batch 64, dimension 384 | 66.64 ms | 1.47 ms | 45.25× | 96.86 / 1.87 MiB |
| GIST, batch 128, dimension 768 | 1824.78 ms | 7.85 ms | 232.32× | 771.44 / 7.46 MiB |
| CachedGIST, batch 128, dimension 384, mini-batch 32 | 330.83 ms | 6.69 ms | 49.48× | 193.88 / 4.65 MiB |

The corresponding PyTorch 2.6.0 timing ratios were 47.25×, 233.22× and 48.72×. Saved storage means unique tensor storage retained for autograd, not peak process memory. These component measurements exclude the encoder and cached embedding replay; GPU performance was not measured.

head: e2f543a617bb8caa362f56448e5f170749989c9a
title: Avoid copying unused hidden layers in WeightedLayerPooling
body:
## Change

Select the requested hidden layers before stacking them in WeightedLayerPooling. Stacking every encoder layer first copies unused activations and retains that larger backing storage for backward even though the reduction only reads the selected suffix.

The weighted multiply and reduction keep their existing order. Earlier encoder parameters still receive gradients through the selected hidden states. This is independent of #4303, which registers custom weight tensors.

## Validation

[Exact-base CPU validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43914106445) compares base `9ac7fdb4` and candidate `e2f543a6` on PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**:

- Baseline: **1 failed, 27 passed**; the storage regression exposes retention of all 13 hidden-state copies.
- Candidate plus adjacent pooling tests: **275 passed, 156 skipped** in each environment. Skips are the existing optional-backend and unavailable CUDA cases.
- Independent weighted-mean and connected encoder tests compare outputs, input gradients, trainable weights and all encoder parameter gradients. FP16/BF16 tests preserve the original reduction and rounding exactly; list/tuple inputs, negative layer offsets and missing hidden states are covered.
- All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

The [reproducible benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/blob/a00e2cbbb099b9d5871dfc2654888271771f581d/.validation/st-weighted-layer-benchmark.py) measures full pooling forward/backward with batch 8, 256 tokens, 768 dimensions, float32, one CPU thread, two warmups and seven timed runs. Outputs and selected-layer/weight gradients are bit-identical to baseline.

| PyTorch 2.14.1 case | Before median | After median | Ratio | Unique saved tensor storage |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 13 hidden states, start 4 | 199.65 ms | 156.49 ms | 1.28× | 84.0 → 60.0 MiB |
| 25 hidden states, start 21 | 190.48 ms | 46.70 ms | 4.08× | 156.0 → 30.0 MiB |

PyTorch 2.6.0 measured 2.07× and 4.86× on the same cases. Storage counts unique tensors retained by autograd, not peak process memory. Encoder execution is outside these component measurements; GPU performance was not measured.

head: 3d53efaffdf3e101536af36c0b331f3f5ca17621
title: Keep CSR expanded reconstruction within the latent width
body:
## Change

Bound the internal 4k reconstruction budget by SparseAutoEncoder's hidden dimension. For a valid main budget such as `hidden_dim=8, k=3`, inference works but training currently calls `topk(..., k=12)` and fails with `selected index k out of range`. The expanded reconstruction should use all available latent features when its requested budget exceeds their count.

This changes only the internal expanded budget. The requested main `k` or `max_active_dims` remains unchanged, and invalid main budgets still raise. Auxiliary reconstruction and normalization retain their existing behavior. This is separate from #4111's auxiliary-mask handling and #4017's disabled-auxiliary support.

## Reproduction and validation

The regression includes a complete offline SparseEncoder built from trainable WordEmbeddings, mean Pooling and SparseAutoEncoder, followed by CSRLoss and backward. No external model download is needed for that reproducer.

[Exact-base validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43914106445), independently on PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**:

- Base `9ac7fdb4`: **50 failed, 34 passed** new cases. Failures include the real SparseEncoder training example and valid budgets above one quarter of the latent width.
- Candidate `3d53efaf`: **110 passed, 8 skipped** with the existing CSR module and loss tests. The skips are existing CUDA cases on CPU runners.
- Direct dense reconstruction references compare latent values, normalized/raw reconstructions, reconstruction losses and gradients for float32/float64, configured/per-call budgets, auxiliary enabled/disabled, and budgets below/at/above the expanded boundary.
- Existing invalid-main-budget errors remain covered. All repository pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

head: 0beec3daeabb3f1428cf830768926fef11b3470c
title: Prevent low-precision dot-product overflow in ContrastiveTensionLoss
body:
## Change

Use the existing `pairwise_dot_score` helper for ContrastiveTensionLoss's aligned sentence pairs. Its elementwise multiply and reduction accumulate FP16/BF16 embeddings in float32, including under CPU autocast, while preserving float64 inputs. The current batched matrix multiplication can overflow before BCEWithLogitsLoss receives the logits.

The reproducer is a complete offline SentenceTransformer with trainable WordEmbeddings and mean Pooling. With 128-dimensional FP16 embeddings containing 32, a valid dot product is 131072; the existing implementation produces infinity and an infinite loss for negative pairs. The patch gives the finite reference loss and finite gradients through both encoders. This change is separate from #4211's inferred labels and model-rebinding behavior.

## Validation

[Exact-base CPU validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43916628776) on PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**:

- Base `9ac7fdb4`: **22 failed, 12 passed** new regression cases in each environment.
- Candidate `0beec3da`: **51 passed** including adjacent Contrastive Tension tests in each environment.
- Independent float64 dot-product/BCE references check losses and gradients for FP16, BF16, float32 and float64; ordinary and overflowing input magnitudes; autocast enabled/disabled; and explicit/inferred labels. The real-model reproducer checks both trainable encoders.
- All repository pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

head: dec6a099db9c4b22aff6264161ab200a1c8121ec
title: Reduce transient memory when loading text word embeddings
body:
## Change

Build a contiguous numeric buffer while reading WordEmbeddings text files, then expose that buffer as a NumPy matrix for the existing embedding constructor. This replaces one NumPy allocation per vocabulary entry and the additional stacked matrix. NumPy converts each row's numeric strings directly instead of running Python `float` once per element.

Parsing remains float64 until the existing constructor applies the requested/default PyTorch dtype, preserving float64 defaults and low-precision rounding. Plain/gzip files, header handling, custom separators and tokenizers, maximum vocabulary size, skipped wrong-width rows, padding and empty-file errors retain their current behavior.

## Validation and benchmark

[Exact-base validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43916628776) compares base `9ac7fdb4` and candidate `dec6a099` independently on PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**. All **39 new compatibility cases pass on both base and candidate**; the candidate plus existing WordEmbeddings tests passes **50 cases** in each environment. Tests include a real SentenceTransformer encode, float32/float64 defaults, FP16/BF16 rounding boundaries, non-finite values, signed zero, Unicode numeric strings and malformed input. All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

The [reproducible benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/blob/83e1c683da360ab8d6028721fca1f4eeeaad6656/.validation/st-parser-benchmark.py) times the complete public `WordEmbeddings.from_text_file` call, including construction of the embedding module, with one warmup and three timed runs. File generation is outside timing. Weight and vocabulary SHA-256 digests match exactly before and after.

| PyTorch 2.14.1 input | Before median | After median | Ratio | Traced allocation peak |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5,000 words × 128 dimensions | 144.51 ms | 113.72 ms | 1.27× | 11,341,583 → 6,671,477 bytes |
| 20,000 words × 300 dimensions | 1,332.01 ms | 1,059.36 ms | 1.26× | 100,284,918 → 57,894,204 bytes |

PyTorch 2.6.0 measured 1.27× and 1.21× on these inputs, with the same allocation peaks. Memory is measured by `tracemalloc` in a separate untimed load and covers its tracked Python/NumPy allocations; it is not whole-process RSS or PyTorch allocator memory.

title: Reuse positive-document membership during reciprocal rank fusion evaluation
body:
## Change

Construct one positive-document set per query while evaluating dense, sparse and fused retrieval rankings. Each ranking currently scans the positive list once per retrieved document; large relevance sets make this membership work dominate evaluation.

The original positive list remains the source for normalization and prediction export, including its order and duplicate entries. The lookup set is rebuilt during each evaluation, so edits to samples between calls are reflected immediately. Ranking and tie behavior are unchanged.

[Exact-base CPU validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43916628776) compares base `9ac7fdb4` and candidate `e3e41bae` on PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**. The **5 new compatibility cases pass on base and candidate**; with adjacent tests, the candidate passes **23 tests** in each environment. Cases include one/multiple/no positives, duplicate positive IDs, exact export ordering and repeated evaluation after sample mutation. All repository pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

The [benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/blob/83e1c683da360ab8d6028721fca1f4eeeaad6656/.validation/st-rrf-benchmark.py) measures the full evaluator with deterministic cached retrieval results, metric computation and prediction JSON export, using 20 queries, one warmup and five timed runs. All nine metrics and exported prediction digests match exactly.

head: 6c3835e07bd2f030b014b6b77c851d9560ac0612
title: Avoid repeated queue entries in paraphrase transitive closure
body:
## Change

Use a deque and mark nodes when enqueuing them in ParaphraseMiningEvaluator's transitive-closure traversal. A dense duplicate graph currently adds the same pending nodes repeatedly, then shifts the remaining Python list on every `pop(0)`. The traversal now visits each node once and examines each edge once before filling the required pairwise closure.

The output still contains every duplicate pair in each connected component. Explicit non-duplicate edges and self edges keep their existing behavior. This is independent of #4120, which ensures traversal follows only edges marked as duplicates.

## Validation and benchmark

[Exact-base CPU validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43917708355) compares base `9ac7fdb4` and candidate `6c3835e0` with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**. All **11 new compatibility cases pass on base and candidate**; the candidate plus existing paraphrase-mining evaluator tests passes **25 tests** in each environment. An independent Boolean reachability reference checks chain, star, complete and disconnected graphs, including explicit false edges and self edges. The public constructor's total duplicate count is also verified. All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

The [reproducible benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/blob/d7e657cbd8df4a0d21fbd19e7b2bc533da98ac23/.validation/st-closure-benchmark.py) times the public evaluator constructor with closure enabled, including normalization and duplicate counting, with one warmup and three timed runs. Input graph construction is outside timing. The complete output graph's SHA-256 digest and duplicate count match exactly.

| PyTorch 2.14.1 runner input | Before median | After median | Ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 128-node complete graph | 26.02 ms | 9.05 ms | 2.87× |
| 384-node complete graph | 1,653.85 ms | 81.68 ms | 20.25× |
| 384-node chain | 80.53 ms | 80.61 ms | 1.00× |

The separate PyTorch 2.6.0 runner measured 2.48×, 13.15× and 1.12×, respectively. The sparse chain is dominated by materializing its required all-pairs closure; the improvement targets redundant queue work on denser input graphs.

head: dcf89983f45b9b39e80101f133fa3f6691539264
title: Fix low-precision teacher probability computation in distillation
body:
## Change

Promote half-precision teacher scores before temperature scaling and softmax in DistillKLDivLoss and the multi-vector equivalent. SparseDistillKLDivLoss inherits the dense implementation. The existing float conversion helper retains float64 targets and keeps teacher targets detached.

Finite float16 scores such as `[80, 79]` overflow when divided by a teacher temperature of `0.001`, producing an all-NaN target distribution. Bfloat16 also rounds ordinary teacher probabilities in its narrow mantissa. Promoting after softmax cannot recover those probabilities. This change performs both operations in at least float32 without changing student scoring or the loss definition.

This was identified through source analysis and reproduced with a locally constructed WordEmbeddings encoder and an actual training forward/backward. It is separate from #4288's excluded log-target handling and #4083's optional target normalization.

## Validation

[Exact-base validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43919834477) compares base `9ac7fdb4` and candidate `dcf89983` on CPU with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**. In each environment the new tests produce **26 failures and 35 passes on unchanged base**, then the candidate and adjacent dense, sparse and multi-vector distillation tests produce **122 passes**. All repository pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

The independent float64 KL reference checks losses and student gradients across float16, bfloat16, float32 and float64 teacher targets; temperatures `0.001`, `0.7` and `2.0`; and autocast where applicable. Tests also verify that teacher targets remain detached and unmodified. Sparse tests use the dense activation representation produced during sparse-encoder training.

head: 0fb4f68bc64dc4d5ea9d8f67b4c7c5cf65fa8ca8
title: Prevent half-precision distance-square overflow in contrastive losses
body:
## Change

Accumulate ContrastiveLoss and OnlineContrastiveLoss distance squares in at least float32, while preserving float64. The conversion happens after the configured distance function, so custom distance functions still receive their original embedding dtype. Online hard-pair selection uses the promoted distances as well.

An unnormalized float16 embedding can have a finite Euclidean distance whose square overflows. A distance near `362` is already sufficient. The positive term becomes infinity; multiplying that infinity by a zero negative-pair label can also produce NaN. The same finite inputs have a finite float32 objective and gradient.

This was reproduced with a locally constructed, trainable WordEmbeddings SentenceTransformer using the public loss forward/backward path. It is separate from #4020's hard-pair inclusion rule and #4078's batch-triplet distance implementation.

## Validation

[Exact-base CPU validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43919834477) compares base `9ac7fdb4` and candidate `0fb4f68b` with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**. In both environments the new tests produce **11 failures and 39 passes on unchanged base**; the candidate and existing contrastive tests produce **58 passes**. All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

The reference selects contributing pairs with Python numbers and differentiates their mathematical squared-distance objective in float64. Coverage includes four floating dtypes, ordinary and large distances, mixed labels, all-positive and all-negative batches, custom distances, and real encoder training with the built-in Euclidean metric. Tests check finite loss, finite gradients and agreement with the independent reference.

head: 5551601f25d80340bf9505d225270593013f16d9
title: Vectorize DCG calculation in retrieval evaluation
body:
## Change

Vectorize the discount calculation in InformationRetrievalEvaluator.compute_dcg_at_k. The evaluator currently calls NumPy's scalar log2 once per relevance entry and accumulates each term in Python, for every query and NDCG cutoff. Computing the discount vector and reduction together removes that per-entry Python work. Dense, sparse and multi-vector retrieval evaluators share this implementation.

Empty and non-positive cutoffs retain their zero result. Relevance inputs remain unmodified, and NumPy's dtype promotion preserves extended-precision inputs.

## Validation and benchmark

The successful DCG jobs in [this exact-base validation run](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43921700020) compare base `9ac7fdb4` with candidate `5551601f` on CPU with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**. All **85 new compatibility tests pass on both revisions**. Candidate tests plus the existing dense, sparse and multi-vector retrieval suites produce **103 passes and 2 CUDA skips** in each environment. All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

The [reproducible benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/blob/d52e86f7b80cc9c660026e6403c2b7e9d32ca901/.validation/st-ir-dcg-benchmark.py) times the public compute_metrics method on precomputed rankings: 200 queries, 20 relevant documents per query, all six metric families, and every cutoff through the corpus size. It includes ranking sort and all metric calculations. Embedding and retrieval are outside the timed region. One warmup precedes five timed repetitions.

| PyTorch 2.14.1 CPU input | Before median | After median | Ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 100 documents/query, 7 cutoffs | 65.94 ms | 27.25 ms | 2.42× |
| 1,000 documents/query, 9 cutoffs | 462.08 ms | 125.88 ms | 3.67× |

The independent PyTorch 2.6.0 runner measured 2.48× and 3.63×, respectively. Every returned metric at every cutoff agrees within `1e-13`; DCG tests also compare against a scalar math.fsum reference with graded relevances, short inputs and float32/float64 arrays.

head: b7f9b47c9c0edb6d50a9b4c134ee9a235d95c077
title: Reduce sparse static token-presence storage eightfold
body:
## Change

Store SparseStaticEmbedding's dense token-presence mask as booleans and convert the incoming binary attention mask to that representation before scattering. Token presence is a binary value, but the current mask uses int64 and is retained by autograd for the weight gradient. Boolean storage reduces this retained mask from eight bytes to one byte per vocabulary entry. It also accepts boolean and uint8 attention masks without a scatter dtype error.

The weighted embeddings and residual addition retain their existing dtypes. This targets storage of token presence; #4184 separately addresses repeated-token scatter conflicts.

## Validation and memory measurement

The successful sparse-mask jobs in [this exact-base CPU run](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43921700020) compare base `9ac7fdb4` and candidate `b7f9b47c` with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**. New tests produce **17 failures and 9 passes on base**: sixteen mask-dtype errors and one storage-size assertion. The candidate plus existing SparseStaticEmbedding tests produces **31 passes** in each environment. All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

Coverage includes float16, bfloat16, float32 and float64 weights; int64, boolean and uint8 binary attention masks; residual embeddings; output and weight/residual gradients; and a complete locally constructed SparseEncoder training forward/backward.

The [reproducible benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/blob/d52e86f7b80cc9c660026e6403c2b7e9d32ca901/.validation/st-sparse-static-mask-benchmark.py) uses a 32,768-token vocabulary and 128-token sequences. Saved-tensor hooks measure unique storage retained by the module's forward, rather than process RSS or the whole training graph. Output and weight-gradient SHA-256 digests match exactly before and after.

| Batch size | Before retained mask | After retained mask | Reduction |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 128 | 32 MiB | 4 MiB | 87.5% |
| 512 | 128 MiB | 16 MiB | 87.5% |

Five timed full module forward/backward repetitions after two warmups measured 46.96 → 45.01 ms and 359.46 → 307.06 ms on the PyTorch 2.14.1 CPU runner (1.04× and 1.17×). The separate 2.6.0 runner measured 1.08× and 1.15×. The main benefit is the deterministic eightfold reduction in retained mask storage.

head: 60e76226e91d8a2648d8c1e9ccefa649288a7fb2
title: Stabilize raw-score subtraction and target dtypes in MarginMSE
body:
## Change

Compute teacher and student score differences in at least float32 before MarginMSE, then match the detached teacher margins to the prediction dtype. This applies to dense, inherited sparse, multi-vector and cross-encoder MarginMSE implementations while preserving float64 predictions.

Finite float16 raw teacher scores `[40000, -40000]` have a finite float32 margin, but their subtraction overflows before the current code reaches its dtype conversion. Ordinary half/bfloat16 teacher margins also trigger mixed-dtype MSE backward errors on PyTorch 2.6; float64 cross-encoder predictions have the corresponding problem when their targets are forced to float32. PyTorch 2.14 handles those mixed-dtype backward cases, but the early subtraction still overflows there.

This was identified through source analysis and reproduced with a locally constructed WordEmbeddings encoder's public training forward/backward. This change concerns signed regression margins and their MSE targets; it does not change KL teacher-probability computation or embedding-distillation projection behavior.

## Validation

The candidate is `60e76226` against exact base `9ac7fdb4`:

| CPU environment | New tests on unchanged base | Candidate and adjacent suites |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| [PyTorch 2.6.0](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43921700020/job/133490383483) | 23 failed, 42 passed | 225 passed, 6 skipped |
| [PyTorch 2.14.1](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43922894820/job/133494562607) | 4 failed, 61 passed | 225 passed, 6 skipped |

The independent float64 reference checks signed-margin losses and gradients across four teacher dtypes, both precomputed margins and raw scores, ordinary and large scores, and all four loss families. Tests also check target detachment and unchanged inputs. Existing multi-vector and cross-encoder loss suites are included; skips are the existing CPU-only environment exclusions. All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

The initial 2.14 validation job stopped because its harness expected the 2.6 baseline failure count. The linked follow-up records the observed 2.14 baseline and completes candidate validation without changing the candidate or test tolerances.

head: 02fe393c18a24d617819a97d3e22d3a1a8d91726
title: Compute tie-aware ADR target ranks without quadratic comparison tensors
body:
## Change

Compute ADRMSELoss's target ranks with a row sort and two searchsorted bounds instead of constructing two batch-by-document-by-document comparison tensors. The bounds preserve the existing average-rank treatment of ties, padded documents, infinities and NaN labels. Target preparation becomes O(B N log N); the differentiable predicted-rank calculation remains quadratic.

This changes the current tie-aware target path. Earlier double-argsort implementations assigned arbitrary ranks to equal labels and are not reused.

## Validation and benchmark

[Exact-base validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43925134003) compares base `9ac7fdb4` with candidate `02fe393c` on CPU with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**. All **121 new compatibility tests pass on both revisions**. Candidate tests together with the existing CrossEncoder loss tests produce **233 passes and 6 skips** in each environment. All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

The tests compare the public loss and score gradients against an independent per-query Python rank calculation and float64 sigmoid objective. They cover ties, negative labels, padding, infinities, NaNs, four label dtypes, three alpha values, and different minibatch sizes.

The [reproducible benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/blob/71ca95fd68df8c3fe2964e57462829611e764a29/.validation/st-adr-ranks-benchmark.py) runs the public loss forward and backward for four ragged queries using a deterministic score-table CrossEncoder. It includes target preparation and predicted-rank work, with two warmups and five timed repetitions. Transformer inference is outside the measured workload.

| PyTorch 2.14.1 CPU query lengths | Before median | After median | Ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 128, 64, 127, 32 | 0.690 ms | 0.638 ms | 1.08× |
| 512, 256, 511, 128 | 9.836 ms | 9.683 ms | 1.02× |
| 2,048, 1,024, 2,047, 512 | 397.69 ms | 239.89 ms | 1.66× |

The independent PyTorch 2.6.0 runner measured 1.08×, 1.27× and 1.68×, respectively. Losses and gradient SHA-256 digests match exactly in every benchmark case. The benefit grows with the document count; these measurements do not claim a whole-model training speedup.

head: d6d7b7b50a34378cad386378ec63a3b5720e2bff
title: Invert CSR normalization with its stabilized scale
body:
## Change

Use the same stabilized standard deviation for SparseAutoEncoder normalization and reconstruction. LN divides centered inputs by `std + eps`, but currently returns the unstabilized `std`; decode and auxiliary reconstruction then multiply by that smaller value. Even an identity encoder/decoder therefore shrinks nonconstant inputs, substantially when their standard deviation is comparable to epsilon.

Return the actual normalization denominator as the `std` metadata. Existing decode, bias conversion and auxiliary reconstruction paths then use the correct inverse factor. The LN documentation and the auxiliary reconstruction expectation are updated to describe that factor.

This addresses a separate denominator mismatch from #4117, which corrected normalized versus raw reconstruction targets. It preserves that raw-target behavior and makes its inverse transform consistent.

## Validation

[Exact-base validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43925134003) compares base `9ac7fdb4` with candidate `d6d7b7b5` on CPU with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**. The new tests give **30 failures and 8 passes on the unchanged base** in both environments. The candidate plus the existing SparseAutoEncoder module and CSR loss tests gives **64 passes and 8 CUDA skips** in each environment. All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

The 38 new cases cover identity reconstruction at several input scales and epsilon values in float32/float64; a signed identity dictionary through the public forward path; reconstruction input gradients; finite constant-input behavior; and an independent formula for the auxiliary bias conversion. The very-small-variance cases expose the production reconstruction error without relying on random inputs or relaxed tolerances.

head: 8453b7d3bcd77718d8f8d54fbd884ed599676b73
title: Support reversed NumPy embedding views in scoring and retrieval
body:
## Change

Accept negative-stride NumPy embedding views in the shared tensor conversion path. Reversing rows or columns, flipping an embedding array, or using a rotated view currently makes public scoring and retrieval functions raise because PyTorch cannot directly wrap negative strides. Materialize those views before conversion while preserving the zero-copy path for writable arrays with nonnegative strides.

This intentionally extends supported NumPy layouts. The earlier zero-copy implementation preserved the old rejection, and its corresponding compatibility test is updated to the new behavior. Input values, dtype and caller-owned arrays remain unchanged; reversed views produce an independent tensor buffer.

## Validation

The successful NumPy jobs in [this validation run](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43928364207) compare base `9ac7fdb4` with candidate `8453b7d3` on CPU with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**. The 34 new cases give **33 failures and 1 pass on the unchanged base**. Candidate tests plus the existing tensor, similarity and retrieval suites give **423 passes, 39 skips and 1 deselection** in each environment. All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

Coverage includes reversed rows, reversed columns and rotated views; writable and read-only arrays; float16/float32/float64; independent NumPy cosine and dot-product ranking oracles through chunked semantic_search; scalar-reference ragged MaxSim scores; and reversed output from a real offline WordEmbeddings SentenceTransformer. A writable positive-stride control still shares its buffer, and every copied case checks values and lack of aliasing.

head: aae6927d9b99bc52c1f9f42f650c42d9ddcc49d0
title: Batch sparse Qdrant queries to reduce HTTP round trips
body:
## Change

Send sparse Qdrant queries through bounded query_batch_points requests instead of one HTTP request per query. A new `query_batch_size` argument defaults to 64. The coalesced query coordinates are partitioned once into row boundaries, avoiding a full coordinate scan for every query. Results retain their input-query order, including empty sparse rows, and `output_index` keeps returning the original client and collection.

No new dependency is introduced: this uses Qdrant's existing batch Query API from the optional qdrant-client dependency.

## Validation and benchmark

[Exact-base validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43929490264) compares base `9ac7fdb4` with candidate `aae6927d` on CPU with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**, qdrant-client **1.20.0**, and a real Qdrant **1.20.0** HTTP service. The new batch-behavior and parameter-contract tests give **20 failures and 9 passes on the unchanged base**. The candidate plus the existing search-engine tests gives **40 passes** in each environment. All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass. Integration tests use the actual in-memory client with duplicate sparse coordinates, empty rows, single queries, three input dtypes and several batch sizes.

The [reproducible benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/blob/14504e8f4e96201ef7e85c3ca6e5bd30ee818640/.validation/st-qdrant-batch-benchmark.py) times the full public semantic_search_qdrant call against an existing 1,000-document index with 256 vocabulary entries and top-5 retrieval. Embeddings and index creation are outside the timed region; sparse preparation, requests and result formatting are included. One warmup precedes three timed repetitions.

| PyTorch 2.14.1, real HTTP service | Requests before → after | Before median | After median | Ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 32 queries | 32 → 1 | 55.73 ms | 6.37 ms | 8.75× |
| 256 queries | 256 → 4 | 444.03 ms | 46.01 ms | 9.65× |

The independent PyTorch 2.6.0 runner measured 7.21× and 11.63×. Returned document IDs match exactly. Both revisions also match an independent float64 sparse-dot-product ranking oracle; maximum relative score error is `1.34e-7`. Server scores between the separately built indexes differ by at most `3e-7` absolute, so the benchmark records these differences and checks a derived float32 multiply-and-accumulate bound instead of requiring bitwise-identical scores.

The [same-runner in-memory control](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43930174569/job/133520165250) has no HTTP round trips to remove: 32 queries take 151.69 → 155.21 ms, and 256 take 1,225.30 → 1,244.30 ms, a measured 1.5–2.3% slowdown. Its complete result digests match exactly. The principal benefit is remote Qdrant retrieval.
